fields.title: Orbita: Technology Devalued the Advantage
fields.summary: What the product relied on has become available to everyone. Decide what the new concept will be.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will the product rely on, and what will you do in the next quarter?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager of Orbita.
fields.brief/company: Orbita is a fictional service for transcribing and analyzing business meeting recordings: 900 corporate clients, average check of 60 thousand rubles per month.
fields.brief/context: Orbita's main advantage is the quality of Russian speech transcription with industry-specific terminology: five years of work and its own labeled dataset. Over the past six months, two infrastructure providers started offering comparable quality almost for free.
fields.brief/objective: Decide what the product will rely on next.
fields.brief/constraints: Team of 30 people. Runway is one year at current revenue.
fields.brief/task: Choose a strategic direction and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: An advantage lasts only as long as it is hard to replicate
fields.learnTakeaway/body: A technology that was once a differentiator eventually becomes infrastructure, and defending it is the most expensive way to lose. The smart move is the opposite: give it up and see what you have that the customer cannot easily take with them. Usually, this is accumulated data and integrations with other people's processes—things that take years to build and cannot be moved in a single migration.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Orbita's transcription accuracy on industry vocabulary: 94%. New available solutions: 91–93% and growing.

Our cost per minute of transcription is 1.1 ₽, while available solutions cost around 0.2 ₽.

Five years of labeled dataset are devaluing: new models do not require such labeling.

Four new competitors emerged this quarter, all less than a year old. Two offer basic transcription for free.

Orbita's churn is still 4% per year: clients are not leaving yet, but three major ones asked to halve the price upon renewal.

Investment in our own model over five years has been the bulk of the company's expenses.
fields.evidenceCards/1/title: How the product is actually used
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Only 21% of 900 clients download the raw transcription.

What they open more often: the list of decisions and action items — 78% of meetings; search across all company meetings for a period — 64% of users at least once a week.

The average company has accumulated 2,400 meetings over two years. Search runs across this entire history.

Integrations: 61% of clients have Orbita linked to their task tracker — action items go there automatically.

In 14 interviews, when asked what would be painful to lose, no one mentioned transcription quality. Eleven named action items and history.

Among the reasons for choosing the product two years ago, 9 out of 10 mentioned transcription quality.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
CTO: keep investing in the model, '94% vs 92% is noticeable'.

Commercial Director: halve the price and go for volume before it's too late.

One of the PMs: stop maintaining our own model, switch to available infrastructure, and invest the freed-up resources into meeting history and action items.

Founder: 'we need a new big idea', suggests building an assistant that runs the meeting itself.

The board of directors wants a decision by next quarter.

Switching to external infrastructure: 2 months of work, 5x reduction in cost per minute, loss of 1–3 percentage points in accuracy.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Three major clients asked to halve the price, citing free solutions. Two of them actively use action items and search.

Switching to a competitor means losing meeting history: while technically transferable, integrations with tasks in the tracker are lost.

Legal and medical companies (11% of clients) require recordings to stay within the country — the two free solutions do not guarantee this.

Over six months, 14 out of 900 clients left; all were small, and all used only transcription.

New deals are harder to close: the sales cycle grew from 1.5 to 3 months, with free solutions popping up in comparisons.

Demand for an 'assistant that runs the meeting' is not validated in client interviews: we asked, the reaction was lukewarm.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Offload transcription to infrastructure, focus on history and action items
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Stop defending what is no longer an advantage, switch to available infrastructure, and build the concept around the accumulated meeting history and task integrations.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The transition takes two months and reduces the cost per minute by 5x; accuracy drops from 94% to 92% — only four clients out of 900 ask about this during the quarter.
Freed-up money and people go where clients are actually retained: 78% of meetings end with action items, 64% of users search history, and 61% have a tracker integration.
You redefine your unfair advantage: 2,400 accumulated meetings per company and task integrations — these cannot be moved to a competitor, while any model can be used.
Instead of a discount, you offer the three major clients a plan with extended history and project-based analysis; two agree, one negotiates and stays.
For legal and medical clients, you keep the in-country storage option — 11% of the base, which free solutions don't offer.
After two quarters, the sales cycle returns to two months, and sales conversations shift from accuracy to history.
Compromise: five years of work on your own model are written off, which was hard on the CTO.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Keep investing in your own model
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: 94% vs 92% is a noticeable difference, and it's what set us apart for five years. Strengthen the model team and regain the lead.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Over the quarter, accuracy is pushed to 94.6%. Available solutions reach 93% in the same time.
Cost remains 5x higher, and free alternatives pop up more often in deals: the cycle grows from three to four months.
In interviews, no one called transcription quality something that would be painful to lose — this data was available but went unused.
After a year, the runway ends while defending a lead that clients don't notice.
Compromise: resources are spent on maintaining an advantage that the market has stopped paying for, despite clear signals of what actually retains clients.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Clients compare us to free options, sales are stalling. Lower the price and retain the base through volume.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Churn stops, and in the first quarter, this looks like a lifesaver.
Revenue from 900 clients drops almost by half, while cost remains the same: our own model costs 1.1 ₽ per minute vs 0.2 ₽ for available solutions.
The one-year runway no longer lasts a year.
At the same time, two out of three clients who asked for a discount actively use action items and history — meaning they are not staying for the price, and could have been offered something else.
Compromise: responding to a free competitor with a price cut while having 5x higher costs is a race you cannot win.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Build an assistant that runs the meeting
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: The founder is right: we need a new big idea, not defense. Dedicate the quarter to an assistant that moderates meetings itself.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The idea is beautiful but is not validated in client interviews: the reaction is lukewarm, no one asked for it.
Four months of team effort go into a direction that has no signs of demand other than the founder's enthusiasm.
During this time, costs are not reduced, meeting history is not strengthened, and the sales cycle continues to grow.
At the same time, the technology itself is applicable: limitations are known, costs are clear — but the limitation it addresses does not bother clients.
Compromise: the bet is placed on technology rather than a customer limitation; exactly the mistake that trend analysis warns against.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: The concept does not highlight the assumption upon whose failure everything collapses
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Technology is evaluated on its own, not by the limitation it removes
